title: Bix's piano thinking in his cornet solos
summary: Hug says Bix's cornet harmonies came from the piano, citing Sweet Sue; Whiteman's 1928 visit.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Well, Armin, can you see shades of his piano playing in his cornet solos? Or are they completely different kinds of things, the cornet solos?

Oh, yeah. Yes, definitely. I can see where basically he thought of the cornet. Always he was thinking of the piano when he was playing the cornet. You see, I'm sure that his harmonies and everything was based on the piano chords. You see, everything. Because he knew the piano harmonies is one of the things that are so fantastic that he knew. You take those harmonies that he has in his inner mist and all those piano things that he made. It's just unbelievable the things that he had in those days. And I'm sure that he based all of his cornet solos around that. He was thinking at times.
Would you even think he'd work them out on the piano maybe before he played them?
I think he worked a lot. I think he worked a great deal of that out first before he made them. Especially when he recorded, I'm sure.
What numbers come to your mind in that? What would you venture to say?

I would say that, I would think just offhand, I can think of one right now. A sweet suit that he made with Paul Whiteman, the big orchestra. Right. That middle, the bridge, when he came to the bridge. And he made that phrase that he wound up on a ninth change. You see, he came down.

And he hit a ninth change right there. Yes. That fits perfect on the piano. I mean, it just falls. Would you do it? Sure. It just, you know that he had to think of that on the piano. There's no other way. Now, I'm sure when he played it spontaneously or improvised, you know, just offhand, offhand, that it was a thing that he didn't have to work anything. Like that meeting we had at the time I saw him at the St. Charles Theater here. Oh, yeah. In 1928 when they played Dinah. Now, there's a tune that not too many people play. I mean, I know, but they picked that out and they played it. And when he started that thing off, everybody in the show was stomping their feet and clapping their hands, you know. I mean, it gives you an idea how we electrify the audience. And the audience was, I'm sure, 99% musicians.

In those days, let's face it, Paul Whiteman was not the most popular favorite amongst the everyday people. You know, it was mostly musicians. That's interesting. And when musicians knew that that mix was in that band and drummer was in that band, that filled up the theater. Well, I mean, you know, you have to realize that this man had reached, I would say that the man had reached his peak. Mm-hmm. At 28. Yeah. That's when he came here. That's when he came here. Because after that, he was on the downgrade. He went downhill then. Yeah. Yeah. But he had reached his peak in 28. Yeah. He was really going strong and going big.
